title: Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

summaries.example: Imagine that nobody had ever invented the number 5 or spoken about it. A mathematical platonist might say that 5 would still exist and that facts about it would still be true. A different philosopher might say that numbers depend in some way on people and their activities.
summaries.summary: Mathematical platonism is a way of thinking about mathematics. It says that mathematical objects, such as numbers and sets, really exist. They are abstract: they do not sit in a particular place or time, and they do not push or pull physical things. Platonism also says these objects do not depend on humans, our words, or our ideas. On this view, mathematicians discover truths about numbers rather than inventing those truths. For example, the fact that 2 + 2 = 4 would not become true only because people wrote it down. A famous argument connected with the philosopher Gottlob Frege starts with how mathematics seems to work. Mathematical sentences appear to talk about objects, and many mathematical theorems are true. The argument says that true sentences of this kind need the words and number-talk to succeed in referring to mathematical objects. Critics raise important questions. If mathematical objects are outside space and time, how can people know about them? Other philosophers think mathematical language can be useful and truth-like without requiring a world of abstract objects. The entry also distinguishes platonism from weaker views. Someone may accept that abstract mathematical objects exist but deny that they are fully independent of thinkers. Someone may also accept that mathematical statements have objective truth-values without believing in mathematical objects at all.
key_ideas: Platonism says that numbers, sets, and other mathematical objects are real in an abstract way.
It says mathematical truths are discovered rather than made up by people.
A famous argument says that because mathematics talks about objects and many mathematical statements are true, mathematical objects must exist.
Some philosophers object that abstract objects seem hard to know about or difficult to understand.
Being a mathematical realist does not automatically mean accepting every part of platonism.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks what reality contains and how knowledge is possible. If platonism is right, reality includes more than physical things such as rocks and stars. It also includes abstract mathematical objects. That would make mathematical knowledge especially puzzling, because abstract objects cannot affect our senses in the ordinary way. The debate also helps us understand why mathematics can be used so successfully in science while philosophers still disagree about what numbers are.

important_terms.definition: The view that mathematical objects exist, are abstract, and do not depend on people or their language and thoughts.
Something that is not located in space or time and cannot cause physical events.
The idea that numbers, sets, and other mathematical things exist.
The view that there are no abstract objects.
The idea that a mathematical statement has one objective truth or falsehood, whether or not we can discover it.

questions_to_think_about: If people disappeared, would facts about numbers still be true?
Are numbers more like planets, or more like rules in a game?
How could people learn about things that cannot be seen or touched?
Can a statement be true even if there are no objects that it seems to mention?

summaries.example: Consider a theorem such as the claim that there are prime numbers between 10 and 20. Mathematical platonism treats this as a statement about an objective mathematical reality: the relevant numbers exist abstractly, and their properties make the statement true. A nominalist might instead accept the theorem's truth while explaining its meaning without committing to abstract numbers. Thus agreement about the theorem does not settle the metaphysical dispute.
summaries.summary: Mathematical platonism is a metaphysical position formed from three theses. First, mathematical objects exist. Second, they are abstract: they lack spatiotemporal location and causal powers. Third, they are independent of intelligent agents and of human language, thought, and practice. The view is inspired by Plato's Forms but is not simply a claim about what the historical Plato believed. It is also normally separated from stronger claims about special mathematical insight or the necessity of every mathematical truth. A central defense is the Fregean argument. It begins with Classical Semantics, the idea that mathematical names and quantifiers function as if they refer to and range over mathematical objects. It combines this with the claim that accepted mathematical theorems are true. If a true theorem must succeed in the reference and quantification it appears to use, mathematical objects exist. This reasoning can also be expressed through a theory of ontological commitment, though that theory is disputed. The argument does not by itself establish Abstractness or Independence. Object realism accepts the first two theses but not necessarily the third. Truth-value realism is different again: it says mathematical statements have objective truth-values but does not explain them by appealing to mathematical objects. The most influential challenge concerns epistemic access. If abstract objects are outside space and time and cannot causally affect us, how can mathematicians be reliable? Defenders may seek non-causal explanations, while critics may regard the problem as serious. A further metaphysical challenge, associated with Benacerraf, argues that mathematics may describe structures without determining which objects occupy their positions. key_ideas: The standard definition combines Existence, Abstractness, and Independence; these claims should be kept distinct.
Object realism is weaker than full platonism because it accepts abstract objects but leaves Independence open.
Truth-value realism concerns objective truth and does not by itself require a realm of mathematical objects.
The Fregean argument depends on claims about how mathematical language works and on the truth of accepted mathematical theorems.
A major objection asks how human mathematicians can reliably know truths about causally isolated abstract objects.
Intermediate positions explore counterfactual independence, many mathematical universes, semantic values, potential existence, or dependence on more basic facts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Platonism has consequences for metaphysics and the theory of knowledge. It conflicts with the idea that reality is exhausted by the physical, since it adds causally inactive abstract objects. It also creates an epistemological challenge: mathematical knowledge would be knowledge of entities that cannot interact with us in ordinary causal ways. The issue matters especially because mathematics is highly successful both as a discipline and as a tool in empirical science. Philosophers therefore cannot easily dismiss mathematics when its metaphysical implications seem surprising. The debate also clarifies whether realism is about objects, truth, language, or mathematical practice.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical view that mathematical objects exist, are abstract, and are independent of intelligent agents, language, thought, and practice.
The claim that mathematical objects exist; examples include numbers, sets, and functions.
The claim that mathematical objects are non-spatiotemporal and therefore causally ineffective.
The claim that mathematical objects do not depend on intelligent agents or their language, thoughts, and practices.
The view that abstract mathematical objects exist, without also claiming that they are independent of thinkers.
The view that well-formed mathematical statements have unique, objective truth-values, even apart from our ability to know them.
The view that there are no abstract objects, in the contemporary philosophical use of the term.

A general form of argument: mathematical language appears to refer to objects, many mathematical theorems are true, and therefore mathematical objects must exist if that language works as it appears to.

questions_to_think_about: Does ordinary mathematical language genuinely refer to objects, or might its apparent reference be misleading?
Would reliable mathematical belief require a causal connection to mathematical objects?
Can object realism be defended without the stronger claim that mathematical objects resemble physical objects in independence?
Does a structural description determine what mathematical objects are, or only how they relate to one another?
Should mathematics be evaluated by standards outside mathematics, such as logic or empirical science, or by its own practices?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “There are prime numbers between 10 and 20.” A platonist hears this as a claim about real but abstract objects: numbers exist whether or not anyone is thinking about them. A nominalist may agree that the sentence is true while saying that it does not require numbers to exist as abstract objects. The two students agree about the math but disagree about what makes the statement true.
summaries.summary: Mathematical platonism says that mathematics is about a realm of abstract objects. Numbers, sets, and functions exist, but they are not located anywhere in space or time and do not cause physical events. The view adds that these objects are independent of human beings, our language, and our mathematical activities. Therefore, mathematical truths are discovered rather than created. The term is connected historically with Plato's theory of Forms, but the modern philosophical position is defined independently of Plato's own views. One important defense is called the Fregean argument. Mathematical language seems to use names for mathematical objects and quantifiers that range over them. Since many mathematical theorems are true, the argument says that this apparent reference must succeed; otherwise the true sentences could not work as they do. This argument depends on controversial assumptions about language and truth. Some philosophers reject the idea that mathematical expressions must refer to objects in the ordinary way. The entry separates several positions that are often confused. Object realism accepts abstract mathematical objects but does not necessarily say they are independent of people. Truth-value realism says that mathematical statements have definite, objective truth-values, but it does not require mathematical objects to explain those truth-values. Nominalists may accept the truth of familiar mathematical sentences while explaining them without abstract numbers. A major criticism of platonism is the problem of knowledge. Mathematicians seem reliable, yet abstract objects would be outside space and time and unable to cause our beliefs. Another criticism questions whether mathematical structures identify particular objects. The entry also discusses intermediate
key_ideas: Platonism treats numbers and sets as real abstract objects, not merely human inventions.
It has three parts: existence, abstractness, and independence.
The Fregean argument connects the way mathematical language works with the truth of mathematical theorems.
Critics ask how we can gain knowledge of objects that cannot affect us physically.
Object realism and truth-value realism show that realism about mathematics can take different forms.
Some philosophers defend views between ordinary object realism and strong platonism.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it connects ordinary mathematics to large questions about reality and knowledge. If platonism is true, the world is not only made up of physical things; it also includes abstract mathematical objects. That raises the question of how people can know about things they cannot see or touch. The debate also shows why two people can agree that a theorem is true while disagreeing about what makes it true. Mathematics can be useful and objective without everyone agreeing on its underlying philosophy.

important_terms.definition: The view that mathematical objects exist, are abstract, and are independent of human thinkers, language, and practices.
An object that is not located in space or time and cannot cause physical events.
The claim that numbers, sets, and functions exist as mathematical objects.
The claim that mathematical objects do not depend on people or their ways of thinking and speaking.
The view that abstract mathematical objects exist, without adding the claim that they are independent of us.
The view that mathematical sentences have objective truth or falsehood, even when people cannot prove or know them.
The contemporary view that there are no abstract objects.
An argument saying that mathematical language appears to refer to objects and that true mathematical theorems therefore support the existence of those objects.

questions_to_think_about: If nobody had ever existed, would 7 still be prime? Why or why not?
Does using a word like “number” prove that numbers exist?
Could people know truths about something that cannot cause any event in the physical world?
Is a true mathematical statement always a statement about an object?
What is the difference between discovering a rule and inventing a rule?
